IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__Connective Tissue:
Autoantibodies help diagnose and classify autoimmune connective tissue disease and vasculitis. Interpret them with the clinical picture — many are non-specific or occur in healthy people, so a positive test supports rather than proves a diagnosis.
1ANA — the screening test
ANA (antinuclear antibody) is the screen for connective tissue disease (especially SLE). It is sensitive but non-specific — also positive in healthy/elderly people and other conditions.
A positive ANA → look at the titre and pattern, then send specific antibodies (ENA, anti-dsDNA). Patterns: homogeneous → dsDNA/SLE; speckled → ENA; nucleolar → scleroderma; centromere → limited SSc. Connective tissue diseases ›
2Key antibody → disease
Anti-dsDNA→SLE — specific; correlates with activity and lupus nephritis.
ANCA→Vasculitis: cANCA/PR3 → GPA; pANCA/MPO → MPA, EGPA. Vasculitis ›
Rheumatoid factor (RF)→Rheumatoid arthritis (also Sjögren’s, healthy people) — non-specific.
Anti-CCP→Rheumatoid arthritis — specific and prognostic (erosive disease). Rheumatoid arthritis ›
AMA (anti-mitochondrial)→Primary biliary cholangitis. PBC ›
ASMA / anti-LKM→Autoimmune hepatitis (type 1 ASMA; type 2 anti-LKM). Autoimmune hepatitis ›
3Interpreting principles
  • A positive test supports, it does not diagnose — the titre and clinical context matter.
  • Some track disease activity (anti-dsDNA in SLE).
🚩
ANCA-associated vasculitis with a pulmonary-renal syndrome (rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis + alveolar haemorrhage) is an emergency → urgent renal/rheumatology input and immunosuppression. Vasculitis ›
📷 Image placeholder — an autoantibody → disease map (ANA screen → ENA/dsDNA; ANCA vasculitis; RF/CCP in RA; AMA/ASMA/LKM in liver disease).
🎓 Exam pearl. ANA = screen for CTD (sensitive, non-specific). Anti-dsDNA = SLE (specific, activity). ANCA = vasculitis (PR3/cANCA → GPA; MPO/pANCA → MPA/EGPA). Anti-CCP = RA (specific). AMA = PBC; ASMA/LKM = autoimmune hepatitis.
The extractable nuclear antigen (ENA) panel is sent after a positive ANA to pin down the specific connective tissue disease. Each antibody carries a characteristic association.
1ENA antibody → disease
Anti-Ro (SSA) / anti-La (SSB)→Sjögren’s (also SLE). Anti-Ro crosses the placenta → neonatal lupus / congenital heart block.
Anti-Sm (Smith)→SLE — highly specific.
Anti-Scl-70 (topoisomerase)→Diffuse systemic sclerosis — risk of lung fibrosis and renal crisis.
Anti-centromere→Limited systemic sclerosis (CREST) — risk of pulmonary hypertension.
Anti-Jo-1→Polymyositis / dermatomyositis (antisynthetase syndrome — ILD, mechanic’s hands).
Anti-U1-RNP→Mixed connective tissue disease.
Some assays miss anti-Ro-positive lupus/Sjögren’s with a negative ANA — request Ro specifically if suspicion is high.
2Scleroderma: diffuse vs limited
🌡️Anti-Scl-70 → diffuse
Widespread skin; lung fibrosis and scleroderma renal crisis. Connective tissue disease ›
🖐️Anti-centromere → limited
CREST (calcinosis, Raynaud’s, oesophageal, sclerodactyly, telangiectasia); risk of pulmonary hypertension.
3Anti-Ro in pregnancy
Anti-Ro (and anti-La) cross the placenta → risk of neonatal lupus and congenital complete heart block. Pregnant anti-Ro-positive women need fetal cardiac monitoring.
🚩
Scleroderma renal crisis (diffuse/anti-Scl-70): accelerated hypertension + AKI → treat with an ACE inhibitor. Antisynthetase (Jo-1) disease → progressive interstitial lung disease.
🎓 Exam pearl. ENA follows a positive ANA. Ro/La → Sjögren’s (Ro → neonatal lupus/heart block). Sm → SLE (specific). Scl-70 → diffuse scleroderma (lung fibrosis/renal crisis); centromere → limited/CREST (pulmonary HTN). Jo-1 → myositis/antisynthetase (ILD). U1-RNP → MCTD.
Anti-CCP and rheumatoid factor (RF) are the serological markers of rheumatoid arthritis — used for diagnosis, prognosis and classification. RA remains a clinical diagnosis.
1The two markers
🎯Anti-CCP
Specific for RA; can precede symptoms; a marker of erosive/severe disease (prognostic). Rheumatoid arthritis ›
🔬Rheumatoid factor
IgM against the Fc of IgG — sensitive but non-specific (also Sjögren’s, other CTD, chronic infection, healthy elderly).
2Use in RA
  • Serology sits alongside inflammatory markers (ESR/CRP) and imaging (X-ray hands/feet for erosions; USS for synovitis) — RA is a clinical diagnosis supported by these.
  • Both feed the ACR/EULAR classification criteria; seropositive (RF and/or anti-CCP) vs seronegative RA.
  • Anti-CCP positivity → worse prognosis (erosions, extra-articular disease) → earlier, more aggressive DMARDs; combined RF + anti-CCP positivity carries the highest risk.
3RF caveats
A positive RF alone does not diagnose RA. It is also raised in Sjögren’s (high titre), SLE, chronic infections (endocarditis, hepatitis C), sarcoidosis, and healthy elderly people.
🚩
RA is a clinical diagnosis — early DMARDs prevent irreversible joint damage. Do not delay referral awaiting serology; refer persistent synovitis urgently, and remember seronegative RA exists (~20–30%). Rheumatoid arthritis ›
🎓 Exam pearl. Anti-CCP = specific for RA, prognostic (erosive) and can precede disease. RF = sensitive but non-specific (Sjögren’s, infections, elderly). Seronegative RA exists. Both feed the ACR/EULAR criteria — but treat early on clinical grounds.
Antiphospholipid antibodies define antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) — thrombosis and/or pregnancy morbidity. Three tests: lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti-β2-glycoprotein I.
1The three tests
🩸Lupus anticoagulant (LA)
A functional clotting test — prolongs the APTT in vitro but causes thrombosis in vivo (paradox); does not correct on mixing.
🧪Anticardiolipin (aCL)
IgG/IgM antibodies against cardiolipin.
🧬Anti-β2-glycoprotein I
IgG/IgM — the most specific of the three.
2Diagnosing APS (Sydney criteria)
  • Clinical: vascular thrombosis (arterial or venous) or pregnancy morbidity (recurrent miscarriage, late fetal loss, severe pre-eclampsia). VTE ›
  • Lab: one of the three antibodies positive on two occasions ≥12 weeks apart (persistence).
  • May be primary or secondary to SLE. Connective tissue disease ›
3Clues & management
  • Clues: recurrent VTE/arterial thrombosis (stroke in the young), recurrent miscarriage, thrombocytopenia, livedo reticularis, an unexplained prolonged APTT, and a false-positive syphilis serology (VDRL/RPR).
  • Thrombosis → lifelong anticoagulation (warfarin; DOACs less effective, especially if triple-positive). Pregnancy → aspirin + LMWH.
🚩
Catastrophic APS (widespread microthrombi → multi-organ failure) is rare and life-threatening. A clue on the bench: an unexplained prolonged APTT that does not correct on mixing, in a patient who clots rather than bleeds → suspect a lupus anticoagulant.
🎓 Exam pearl. APS = thrombosis + pregnancy morbidity + persistent antiphospholipid antibodies (LA, aCL, anti-β2GPI) ≥12 weeks apart. Lupus anticoagulant paradox: prolongs the APTT but causes clotting. Treat thrombosis with warfarin (not a DOAC if triple-positive); pregnancy with aspirin + LMWH.
Complement (C3, C4, CH50) is measured in immune-complex / consumption diseases. Low levels indicate consumption (active disease); a very low CH50 screens for a component deficiency.
1What they measure
  • C3 and C4 — individual components; consumed in immune-complex disease.
  • CH50 (total haemolytic complement) — tests the whole classical pathway; a very low/absent CH50 suggests a component deficiency.
  • Complement is also an acute-phase reactant, so consumption can be partly masked in inflammation.
2Low complement → disease
Low C3 and C4→Active SLE (classical-pathway/immune-complex; tracks activity & nephritis). SLE ›
Low C3, normal C4→Alternative-pathway activation → post-streptococcal GN (transient), or a C3 nephritic factor in MPGN / C3 glomerulopathy. Glomerulonephritis ›
Low C4 (± low C1-INH)→Hereditary angioedema (C1-inhibitor deficiency) — a low C4 is the screening clue; confirm with a C1-inhibitor level and function.
Also low in→Cryoglobulinaemia, membranoproliferative GN, infective endocarditis.
3Complement deficiency
🧬Early classical (C1, C2, C4)
Deficiency → an SLE-like disease (impaired immune-complex clearance).
🦠Terminal (C5–9 / MAC)
Deficiency → recurrent Neisseria (meningococcal) infection. Meningococcal disease ›
🚩
Recurrent Neisseria / meningococcal infections → test complement (terminal pathway / CH50) and vaccinate. Hereditary angioedema (low C4) → airway swelling without urticaria; it does not respond to adrenaline/antihistamines — give C1-inhibitor concentrate (do not mistake it for anaphylaxis).
📷 Image placeholder — the complement cascade (classical / alternative / terminal) annotated with which diseases consume or lack each part.
🎓 Exam pearl. Low C3/C4 = consumption — active SLE (tracks activity) and immune-complex GN. Low C3 + normal C4 = alternative pathway (post-strep GN). Low C4 → hereditary angioedema (C1-INH deficiency). CH50 screens the classical pathway; terminal deficiency → recurrent Neisseria.
IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__Rheumatology & HL:
HLA-B27 is an MHC class I allele strongly associated with the seronegative spondyloarthropathies. It is present in ~8% of healthy people, so it supports a diagnosis but does not confirm it.
1Associated conditions (PAIR)
Psoriatic arthritisAnkylosing spondylitis (strongest, ~90%)IBD-associated (enteropathic)Reactive arthritis
All are “seronegative” (RF and ANA negative). Seronegative spondyloarthropathies › Reactive arthritis follows a GI/GU infection — the triad of arthritis, urethritis and conjunctivitis.
2Shared extra-articular features
Enthesitis (e.g. Achilles)Dactylitis (sausage digit)Anterior uveitisAortic regurgitationApical lung fibrosis (AS)
3Clinical use
  • Supports axial spondyloarthritis alongside inflammatory back pain and MRI sacroiliitis — part of the ASAS classification criteria.
  • A positive test supports; a negative does not exclude — not a stand-alone diagnostic test.
🚩
Inflammatory back pain in a young adult (worse at rest, better with activity, morning stiffness >30 min, onset <45 years) → consider axial SpA. Anterior uveitis (painful red eye, photophobia) needs urgent ophthalmology. Uveitis ›
📷 Image placeholder — HLA-B27 spondyloarthropathy features: sacroiliitis and “bamboo spine” on X-ray, dactylitis and enthesitis.
🎓 Exam pearl. HLA-B27 = seronegative spondyloarthropathies (PAIR: Psoriatic, Ankylosing spondylitis, IBD-associated, Reactive). Strongest with ankylosing spondylitis (~90%). Present in ~8% of healthy people → supports, doesn’t diagnose. Features: enthesitis, dactylitis, anterior uveitis.
HLA-B51 is associated with Behçet’s disease — a systemic vasculitis characterised by recurrent oral and genital ulcers. HLA-B51 supports the diagnosis, which is clinical.
1Behçet’s features
Recurrent oral ulcers (required)Genital ulcersUveitis (can blind)Skin: erythema nodosum, pathergyArthritisGI / neuro / vascular (VTE, aneurysm)
2The pathergy test
Pathergy — a papule/pustule forming after a needle prick (skin hyper-reactivity) — is characteristic and supports the diagnosis.
3Diagnosis
  • Clinical criteria: recurrent oral ulcers plus two of: genital ulcers, eye lesions, skin lesions, or a positive pathergy test.
  • More common along the Silk Road (Turkey, Middle East, East Asia). Vasculitis ›
4Management
  • Colchicine for mucocutaneous disease; corticosteroids and immunosuppression (azathioprine, biologics) for major-organ involvement.
  • Behçet’s uniquely affects both arteries and veins of any size; its venous thrombosis is treated with immunosuppression, not anticoagulation alone.
🚩
Behçet’s posterior/panuveitis is sight-threatening; neuro-Behçet’s and large-vessel disease (aneurysm, venous thrombosis) are serious → urgent specialist input. Uveitis ›
🎓 Exam pearl. HLA-B51 = Behçet’s disease. Recurrent oral + genital ulcers, uveitis, pathergy. Silk Road distribution. HLA supports; the diagnosis is clinical.
Many autoimmune diseases carry HLA associations — mostly supportive (the alleles are common), but a few are high-yield exam facts. Here are the classic ones by class I and class II.
1Class I (A, B, C)
HLA-B27→Ankylosing spondylitis & spondyloarthropathies (PAIR).
HLA-B51→Behçet’s disease.
HLA-A3→Haemochromatosis (HFE).
HLA-Cw6→Psoriasis.
HLA-B*57:01→Abacavir hypersensitivity — a pharmacogenetic screen done BEFORE prescribing abacavir (HIV); if positive, avoid the drug.
2Class II (DR, DQ)
HLA-DR3→SLE, Sjögren’s, Graves’, autoimmune hepatitis, coeliac, Addison’s, T1DM.
HLA-DR4→Rheumatoid arthritis, T1DM. RA ›
HLA-DR3 + DR4→Type 1 diabetes (highest risk). T1DM ›
HLA-DQ2 / DQ8→Coeliac disease — near-universal; a negative DQ2/DQ8 makes coeliac very unlikely (high NPV). Coeliac ›
HLA-DR2 / DR15→Goodpasture’s, narcolepsy (its DQB1*06:02 is the strongest known HLA–disease link), MS, SLE.
🚩
Most HLA alleles are population-common and only modestly raise risk — use them as supportive, not diagnostic. The main exception with clinical utility is the high negative predictive value of HLA-DQ2/DQ8 for coeliac disease.
📷 Image placeholder — an HLA-association summary grid (class I vs class II alleles mapped to their diseases).
🎓 Exam pearl. B27 → AS/spondyloarthropathy; B51 → Behçet’s; A3 → haemochromatosis; Cw6 → psoriasis; B*57:01 → screen before abacavir. DR3 → SLE/Sjögren’s/Graves’/AIH/coeliac/Addison’s; DR4 → RA/T1DM; DR3+DR4 → T1DM; DQ2/DQ8 → coeliac (high NPV); DR2/DR15 → Goodpasture’s/narcolepsy/MS.
In transplantation, HLA typing and cross-matching match donor and recipient to minimise rejection. ABO compatibility is required, and HLA-A, -B and -DR are the most important loci to match.
1Matching & the cross-match
  • HLA matching (A, B, DR) → better matching means less rejection and longer graft survival.
  • The cross-match detects preformed recipient antibodies against donor HLA (from prior transfusion, pregnancy or transplant). A POSITIVE cross-match is a contraindication (hyperacute rejection risk).
2Rejection types
⚡Hyperacute (mins–hrs)
Preformed antibodies (ABO/HLA) → thrombosis. Prevented by the cross-match — not treatable.
📅Acute (weeks)
T-cell mediated (cellular) ± antibody-mediated → treat with immunosuppression.
🕰️Chronic (months–yrs)
Progressive fibrosis and vascular change → graft dysfunction. Transplant immunology ›
3Sensitisation & monitoring
  • Panel reactive antibody (PRA) — the % of the population the recipient has HLA antibodies against; a high PRA = highly sensitised and harder to match.
  • Donor-specific antibodies (DSA) are monitored post-transplant (antibody-mediated rejection). A virtual cross-match uses the antibody screen against the donor type.
  • Maintenance immunosuppression (calcineurin inhibitor + antimetabolite + steroid) prevents acute rejection, but over-suppression risks opportunistic infection (CMV, PCP) and malignancy (PTLD, skin cancer).
🚩
Hyperacute rejection is prevented, not treated — an ABO and HLA cross-match before transplant is mandatory. Note: in bone-marrow/stem-cell transplant (and with non-irradiated cellular blood products in the immunocompromised), the risk is reversed — graft-versus-host disease.
🎓 Exam pearl. Match HLA-A/B/DR + ABO. The cross-match detects preformed anti-donor HLA antibodies — a positive cross-match contraindicates (hyperacute rejection). PRA = degree of sensitisation. Rejection: hyperacute (preformed Ab) → acute (T-cell) → chronic (fibrosis).
IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__Neuro-immunology:
Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an autoimmune disorder of the postsynaptic neuromuscular junction causing fatigable weakness. The key antibodies are anti-AChR (most) and anti-MuSK.
1The antibodies
🎯Anti-AChR
Antibody to the acetylcholine receptor — positive in ~85% of generalised MG. The main test.
🔬Anti-MuSK
In many AChR-negative MG (often bulbar/respiratory-predominant). A minority are seronegative (anti-LRP4 or none).
2Clinical & other tests
  • Fatigable weakness worse with activity / end of day: ptosis, diplopia, bulbar (dysphagia, dysarthria), proximal limb, respiratory.
  • Support with the ice-pack test, repetitive nerve stimulation (decrement), and single-fibre EMG (most sensitive).
  • CT chest — look for a thymoma or thymic hyperplasia (associated). Neuromuscular junction disorders ›
3Management
  • Symptomatic: pyridostigmine (acetylcholinesterase inhibitor).
  • Immunosuppression (steroids, azathioprine); thymectomy (especially with thymoma).
  • MuSK-positive MG responds poorly to pyridostigmine — rituximab is effective.
🚩
Myasthenic crisis — respiratory failure from bulbar/respiratory weakness → monitor FVC, ICU, and IVIG or plasma exchange. Avoid drugs that worsen MG (aminoglycosides, macrolides, beta-blockers).
📷 Image placeholder — the neuromuscular junction in MG (antibody blockade of the postsynaptic AChR) and a decremental RNS trace.
🎓 Exam pearl. MG = fatigable weakness (ptosis, diplopia, bulbar). Anti-AChR (~85%); anti-MuSK if AChR-negative. Associated thymoma → CT chest. Treat with pyridostigmine + immunosuppression; crisis → FVC + IVIG/PLEX. (Contrast LEMS, which improves with use.)
Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) is an autoimmune disorder of the presynaptic neuromuscular junction — antibodies against voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCC). It is often paraneoplastic (small-cell lung cancer).
1Antibody & mechanism
  • Anti-VGCC (P/Q-type) → reduced presynaptic acetylcholine release → weakness.
  • ~50–60% paraneoplastic — associated with small-cell lung cancer. Lung cancer ›
  • LEMS is one of the paraneoplastic syndromes of SCLC — alongside SIADH and ectopic ACTH (Cushing’s).
2LEMS vs myasthenia
💪Improves with use
Proximal (leg) weakness that IMPROVES with repeated use (post-tetanic potentiation) — the opposite of MG fatigability. Reflexes return after exercise.
🌵Autonomic features
Dry mouth, constipation, impotence. Ocular/bulbar signs are less prominent than in MG.
3Investigations
  • Anti-VGCC antibodies.
  • Repetitive nerve stimulation: an INCREMENT at high frequency (opposite to MG’s decrement).
  • Screen for small-cell lung cancer — CT chest ± PET.
4Management
  • Treat the underlying cancer. Symptomatic: 3,4-diaminopyridine (amifampridine); immunosuppression as needed.
🚩
LEMS may precede the cancer diagnosis by months to years → actively screen for small-cell lung cancer and re-screen if the initial work-up is negative. Lung cancer ›
🎓 Exam pearl. LEMS = presynaptic, anti-VGCC, paraneoplastic (SCLC). Proximal weakness that IMPROVES with use; autonomic features; reflexes return after exercise. RNS shows an INCREMENT (MG shows a decrement). Screen for SCLC.
Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) is an autoimmune demyelinating disease distinct from MS — antibodies against aquaporin-4 (AQP4) or MOG. The distinction matters because some MS drugs worsen NMO.
1The antibodies
💧Anti-aquaporin-4 (AQP4-IgG)
The defining antibody of NMOSD — targets the astrocyte water channel.
🧫Anti-MOG
MOG-antibody disease (MOGAD) — an overlapping but distinct entity (often more monophasic, ADEM-like, better prognosis).
2Clinical features
Optic neuritis (often severe / bilateral)Longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (≥3 segments)Area postrema syndrome (intractable hiccups / vomiting)
3NMO vs MS
  • NMO: AQP4-IgG positive, longitudinally extensive myelitis, severe optic neuritis; CSF oligoclonal bands usually NEGATIVE.
  • MS: shorter cord lesions, typical brain lesions, oligoclonal bands positive. Multiple sclerosis ›
4Management
  • Acute: high-dose steroids and plasma exchange.
  • Prevention: immunosuppression (rituximab, and NMOSD-specific biologics — eculizumab, satralizumab, inebilizumab) — NOT MS disease-modifying drugs.
🚩
Longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis or severe/bilateral optic neuritis → test AQP4 / MOG and do not treat as MS: some MS therapies (interferon, natalizumab) worsen NMO. Multiple sclerosis ›
🎓 Exam pearl. NMOSD = AQP4-IgG (astrocyte water channel); optic neuritis + longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis. Oligoclonal bands usually NEGATIVE (vs MS positive). MOG-antibody disease is related but distinct. Don’t use MS drugs — treat with steroids/PLEX + immunosuppression.
Anti-GQ1b antibodies are associated with Miller Fisher syndrome — a variant of Guillain–Barré syndrome. GQ1b ganglioside is enriched in the nerves controlling eye movements.
1Miller Fisher syndrome
  • Triad: ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and areflexia.
  • Anti-GQ1b antibodies (GQ1b is enriched in cranial nerves III/IV/VI).
  • Often post-infectious — classically Campylobacter jejuni. Guillain–Barré syndrome ›
2Relation to GBS
GBS = ascending flaccid paralysis with areflexia, usually post-infectious (Campylobacter, CMV, EBV). Miller Fisher is a variant (a descending/cranial pattern) — anti-GQ1b is its marker.
3Investigations
  • Anti-GQ1b antibodies (Miller Fisher).
  • CSF: albuminocytological dissociation — raised protein with a normal cell count.
  • Nerve conduction studies; monitor FVC (respiratory) and autonomic function.
🚩
In GBS, watch for respiratory failure (serial FVC — not oxygen saturation, which falls late) and autonomic instability (arrhythmia, labile BP) → ICU. Treat with IVIG or plasma exchange. Miller Fisher generally has a good prognosis. Guillain–Barré syndrome ›
🎓 Exam pearl. Anti-GQ1b = Miller Fisher syndrome — ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia; a GBS variant, often post-Campylobacter. CSF shows albuminocytological dissociation. Treat with IVIG/PLEX; monitor FVC.
IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__Renal & Post-infe:
Anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture’s) is an autoimmune attack on the glomerular and alveolar basement membrane (type IV collagen) → rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and pulmonary haemorrhage.
1The antibody
  • Anti-GBM antibodies against type IV collagen (α3 chain) in glomerular and alveolar basement membranes.
  • Biopsy shows LINEAR IgG deposition on immunofluorescence. Associated with HLA-DR15.
2Pulmonary-renal syndrome
Rapidly progressive GN (crescentic; haematuria, AKI)Pulmonary haemorrhage (haemoptysis — worse in smokers)
3Investigations
  • Serum anti-GBM antibodies.
  • Renal biopsy: crescentic GN with linear IgG on IF. Glomerulonephritis ›
  • Also check ANCA — ~30% are double-positive (anti-GBM + ANCA). Vasculitis ›
  • The three RPGN immunofluorescence patterns: linear (anti-GBM), granular (immune-complex — lupus, post-strep), pauci-immune (ANCA vasculitis).
4Management
  • Urgent plasma exchange (removes antibody) + immunosuppression (steroids, cyclophosphamide).
🚩
A pulmonary-renal syndrome (haemoptysis + AKI/haematuria) is an emergency → test anti-GBM and ANCA and start plasma exchange urgently. Renal recovery is poor once oligoanuric / dialysis-dependent — treat early.
📷 Image placeholder — renal biopsy immunofluorescence showing smooth linear IgG along the GBM (vs granular in immune-complex GN).
🎓 Exam pearl. Anti-GBM = Goodpasture’s (type IV collagen, α3). Pulmonary-renal syndrome: RPGN + lung haemorrhage. LINEAR IgG on IF. HLA-DR15. Treat with plasma exchange + immunosuppression urgently; check ANCA (double-positive in ~30%).
Anti-PLA2R antibodies are the marker of primary membranous nephropathy — the commonest cause of nephrotic syndrome in (Caucasian) adults.
1The antibody
  • Anti-phospholipase A2 receptor (PLA2R) — positive in ~70–80% of primary membranous nephropathy (a podocyte target antigen).
  • A smaller subset are anti-THSD7A positive.
2Membranous nephropathy
  • Commonest cause of adult nephrotic syndrome. Biopsy: subepithelial immune deposits (“spike and dome”, thickened GBM). Glomerulonephritis ›
  • Primary (anti-PLA2R) vs secondary — malignancy, SLE (class V), hepatitis B, drugs (gold, penicillamine, NSAIDs).
3Using anti-PLA2R
Positive→Supports primary MN; monitors activity/response and predicts relapse.
Negative→Actively look for a secondary cause (malignancy screen in older patients).
4Management context
  • Supportive: ACEi/ARB, diuretics, statin; treat any secondary cause.
  • Immunosuppression — rituximab is now the preferred first-line agent (KDIGO) — for high-risk/persistent nephrotic disease.
🚩
Nephrotic syndrome — membranous especially — carries a high risk of venous thromboembolism and renal vein thrombosis (urinary loss of antithrombin III) → consider anticoagulation in high-risk patients. If anti-PLA2R negative, hunt for a secondary cause (including malignancy).
🎓 Exam pearl. Anti-PLA2R = primary membranous nephropathy (commonest adult nephrotic). Biopsy: subepithelial “spike and dome” deposits. Secondary causes: malignancy, SLE (class V), hepatitis B, drugs. High VTE/renal vein thrombosis risk. Anti-PLA2R negative → hunt a secondary cause.
The antistreptolysin O (ASO) and anti-DNase B titres are serological markers of a recent group A streptococcal (GAS) infection. They do not diagnose active infection — they confirm that a preceding strep infection is the trigger for an immune-mediated post-streptococcal complication, chiefly post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) and acute rheumatic fever (Jones criteria).
1What the two markers are & when to use each
Both are antibodies against GAS exotoxins/enzymes, rising after the infection has often resolved. The site of the original infection determines which is more useful.
🫁ASO
Best marker after pharyngitis / tonsillitis. Rises ~1–3 weeks post-infection, peaks ~3–5 wks. Poorly raised after skin infection.
🩹Anti-DNase B
More reliable after skin infection (impetigo / pyoderma), where ASO is often normal. Rises a little later.
Send both to maximise yield — a single normal ASO does not exclude a streptococcal trigger, especially after skin infection.
2How to interpret the titre
A single raised value only proves prior exposure — titres stay elevated for months and healthy children can have modestly raised baselines. Rising or paired titres (acute + convalescent 2–4 wks apart) are far more informative than one snapshot.
Paired rising titrestrongly supports recent GASASO + anti-DNase B together
Single high ASO, no clinical context→may just reflect past carriage — interpret with caution
3PSGN — the classic nephritic picture
PSGN is a nephritic syndrome appearing after a latent period: ~1–2 weeks after a throat infection or ~3–6 weeks after a skin infection.
  • Visible haematuria — classically "coca-cola" / smoky urine
  • Hypertension and oedema (periorbital, fluid overload)
  • Acute kidney injury with oliguria; mild proteinuria
Complement→Low C3 that normalises by ~6–8 weeks (C4 usually normal)
Biopsy (rarely needed)→subepithelial "humps"; granular IgG/C3 on immunofluorescence
Management is supportive — fluid/salt restriction, antihypertensives, diuretics for overload. It is usually self-limiting, especially in children, with full recovery. See Glomerulonephritis ›.
4Key discriminator: PSGN vs IgA nephropathy
Both present with visible haematuria after an upper respiratory infection, but the timing and complement separate them cleanly — a favourite finals distinction.
⏳PSGN
Latent period of 1–6 wks after infection. Low C3 (normalises). Positive ASO / anti-DNase B.
⚡IgA nephropathy
Synpharyngitic: haematuria within 1–2 days of infection, no latent period, and a normal C3.
Haematuria <48h into a sore throat, normal C3→think IgA nephropathy, not PSGN
🚩
A persistently low C3 beyond 8–12 weeks, worsening AKI, heavy proteinuria/nephrotic features, or a fall in urine output warrants urgent nephrology review and renal biopsy — this points away from simple PSGN toward membranoproliferative GN, lupus nephritis, or crescentic GN.

🎓 Exam pearl. ASO = throat, anti-DNase B = skin — send both. PSGN is nephritic with a latent period and LOW C3 that recovers by 6–8 weeks. If haematuria appears during the infection with a normal C3, it is IgA nephropathy (synpharyngitic). Management of PSGN is supportive and prognosis in children is excellent.
Lyme disease (Borrelia burgdorferi, transmitted by Ixodes ticks) is diagnosed serologically using a two-tier strategy: a sensitive screening ELISA first, confirmed by a specific immunoblot (Western blot). The great trap is timing — antibodies take weeks to appear, so early serology is often falsely negative, and they persist for years, so serology cannot confirm cure. Lyme disease ›
1The two-tier algorithm
Never confirm Lyme on a single ELISA — its high sensitivity comes at the cost of specificity, so false positives are common (cross-reactivity with EBV, syphilis, autoimmune disease).
Step 1: ELISA positive OR equivocal→Step 2: confirmatory immunoblot (IgM & IgG)
Step 1: ELISA negative→No immunoblot; if early disease suspected, repeat serology in 4–6 weeks
ELISA = sensitive screenImmunoblot = specific confirmation
2Match the test to the clinical stage
🎯Early / localised
Erythema migrans — expanding "bull's-eye" rash. Clinical diagnosis — do NOT wait for serology.
🧠Neuroborreliosis
Facial/cranial nerve palsy, meningitis. Serology usually positive; consider paired CSF antibody index.
❤️Lyme carditis
AV heart block (may fluctuate). Serology positive by this stage.
🦴Lyme arthritis
Large-joint (knee) mono/oligoarthritis. Strongly IgG-positive — a negative IgG makes it very unlikely.
By the disseminated/late stages the immune response has matured, so serology is reliably positive — a negative test then argues strongly against Lyme.
3Two caveats that catch candidates out
  • Falsely negative early (the window): antibodies take weeks to develop. A negative test in the first few weeks does not exclude Lyme — repeat in 4–6 weeks if suspicion persists.
  • Stays positive after cure: IgG can persist for years. Serology cannot be used to monitor treatment response or diagnose reinfection — do not "re-check the titre" to prove cure.
Doxycycline first-lineAmoxicillin alternativeCeftriaxone for CNS / cardiac
🚩
Suspected Lyme carditis (syncope, dyspnoea, palpitations with high-degree AV block) or neuroborreliosis needs urgent admission and IV ceftriaxone — do not delay treatment while awaiting immunoblot confirmation.

Thyroid autoantibodies help pin down the cause of thyroid dysfunction once the TFTs tell you the gland is under- or over-active. The two you must know are TPO antibodies (the marker of autoimmune thyroiditis) and TRAb (TSH-receptor antibodies, the driver of Graves' disease). Antibodies support the biochemical diagnosis — they never replace it.
1The two key antibodies
🦋TPO antibodies
Anti-thyroid peroxidase. The marker of autoimmune thyroiditis — high in Hashimoto's (hypothyroid) and often positive in Graves' too. The most useful antibody in hypothyroidism.
⚡TRAb
TSH-receptor antibodies — stimulating antibodies that switch the receptor on, causing Graves' disease and hyperthyroidism. Confirm Graves' when the cause of thyrotoxicosis is unclear.
🧬Thyroglobulin antibodies
A less-used third antibody. Adds little over TPO in most cases; occasionally checked in thyroid cancer follow-up interpretation.
2How to interpret them
Always read antibodies alongside the TFTs — they explain the mechanism, they do not make the diagnosis on their own.
High TSH, low T4 + TPO+→Hashimoto's (autoimmune hypothyroidism)
Low TSH, high T4 + TRAb+→Graves' disease
Thyrotoxicosis, cause unclear→TRAb distinguishes Graves' from thyroiditis
TPO+ predicts progression subclinical → overt hypothyroidismTPO+ raises post-partum thyroiditis risk
3When to request each
  • TPO — confirmed or subclinical hypothyroidism, to establish an autoimmune cause and gauge progression risk.
  • TRAb — thyrotoxicosis to confirm Graves', especially when there is no eye disease and the cause is uncertain.
  • TRAb in pregnancy — in any woman with current or past Graves' disease (see red flag).
Isotope uptake scanning is an alternative when antibodies are equivocal or contraindicated (not in pregnancy).
🚩
Pregnancy: TRAb crosses the placenta. A mother with Graves' — even if euthyroid after treatment, surgery or radioiodine — can have circulating TRAb that stimulates the fetal thyroid, causing fetal and neonatal thyrotoxicosis (tachycardia, goitre, growth restriction). Measure TRAb in these women and arrange fetal monitoring and neonatal follow-up.

TRAb is a stimulating antibody and the only thyroid antibody that matters in pregnancy because it crosses the placenta. Anti-21-hydroxylase (21-OH) antibodies are the serological marker of autoimmune Addison's disease — autoimmune primary adrenal insufficiency, the commonest cause of Addison's in the developed world. They target the adrenal steroidogenic enzyme 21-hydroxylase, confirming an autoimmune aetiology once primary adrenal insufficiency has been diagnosed.
1What the antibody tells you
Anti-21-OH is a disease-defining, not a screening, test. First establish primary adrenal insufficiency biochemically, then use anti-21-OH to label it as autoimmune.
Anti-21-OH positiveAutoimmune Addison's
Primary adrenal insufficiency + anti-21-OH +ve→Autoimmune adrenalitis confirmed
See the underlying condition: Addison's disease ›
2Clinical and biochemical picture
Insidious onset of fatigue, weight loss, anorexia and postural hypotension. Hyperpigmentation (palmar creases, buccal mucosa, scars) reflects high ACTH co-secreted with melanocyte-stimulating peptides.
  • Biochemistry: hyponatraemia + hyperkalaemia (mineralocorticoid loss), ± hypoglycaemia.
  • Confirm the insufficiency with the short Synacthen test (subnormal cortisol rise), plus a 9am cortisol and paired ACTH (high in primary disease).
  • Anti-21-OH then defines the aetiology as autoimmune.
3Autoimmune polyendocrine associations
Autoimmune Addison's is part of the autoimmune polyendocrine syndromes (APS-1 and APS-2) — screen for associated organ-specific autoimmunity.
🩸Type 1 diabetes
Classic APS-2 partner — watch for falling insulin needs.
🦋Autoimmune thyroid
Hashimoto's / Graves' — check TFTs and TPO.
🌾Coeliac disease
Check anti-tTG; contributes to malabsorption.
🔴Pernicious anaemia
B12 deficiency; also vitiligo, a common skin marker.
Cross-check the commonest partner: Type 1 diabetes ›
4Management
Lifelong replacement of both hormone axes:
Hydrocortisone (glucocorticoid)Fludrocortisone (mineralocorticoid)
Educate on sick-day rules, a steroid emergency card, and IM hydrocortisone for emergencies. Never stop steroids abruptly.
🚩
Adrenal (Addisonian) crisis is a medical emergency: hypotension/shock, severe hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia, often triggered by infection or missed doses. Give IV hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately plus IV 0.9% saline — do not delay for test results. Reinforce sick-day rules: double the oral steroid dose during acute illness or fever.

Suspect coeliac disease? The first-line blood test is IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase (anti-tTG IgA) — cheap, highly sensitive and specific. But two things must be right for the result to mean anything: the patient must still be eating gluten, and you must check total IgA at the same time. Get either wrong and a truly coeliac patient can serologically look normal.
1The serology ladder
🌾IgA anti-tTG
First-line. High sensitivity & specificity — the screening test of choice in adults and children.
🔬IgA EMA
Endomysial Ab. More specific — used as a second-line/confirmatory test, e.g. weak-positive tTG.
🧬IgG anti-DGP / IgG-tTG
IgA-deficient route. IgG-based tests (deamidated gliadin peptide, IgG-tTG/EMA) when total IgA is low.
Always request total IgA alongside anti-tTG IgA
2The two great false-negative traps
Gluten-free diet before testing→Serology (& biopsy) normalise → false negative
Selective IgA deficiency→IgA anti-tTG falsely negative → use IgG tests
  • Patient must be on a gluten-containing diet — gluten in more than one meal a day for ≥6 weeks before serology and biopsy.
  • Selective IgA deficiency is over-represented in coeliac; a low total IgA renders IgA-based serology unreliable, so switch to IgG anti-tTG / IgG-DGP / IgG-EMA.
If the patient has already gone gluten-free and refuses to restart, HLA-DQ2/DQ8 testing has a role: a negative result makes coeliac very unlikely.
3From positive serology to diagnosis
A positive anti-tTG IgA does not by itself confirm coeliac. In adults, refer for duodenal biopsy (gold standard) showing villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and raised intraepithelial lymphocytes. Some paediatric pathways allow a no-biopsy diagnosis with high-titre tTG (≥10× ULN) plus positive EMA and HLA-DQ2/DQ8.

🚩
Never let a patient start a gluten-free diet before testing — it normalises both serology and biopsy and can mask the diagnosis for years. If clinical suspicion is high but serology negative, check total IgA and confirm the patient was eating gluten before excluding the diagnosis.

The classic exam trap: coeliac serology is negative but suspicion remains — the answer is almost always "check total IgA" (selective IgA deficiency) or "confirm the patient is on a gluten-containing diet." Serum IgG4 is the serological marker of IgG4-related disease (IgG4-RD), a multi-system fibro-inflammatory condition whose pancreatic prototype is type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis (AIP). A raised level supports but never alone confirms the diagnosis, and the single most important trap is that AIP is a near-perfect mimic of pancreatic cancer.
1What serum IgG4 means (and doesn't)
IgG4 is one of four IgG subclasses; markedly raised serum levels underpin IgG4-RD. It is a supportive, not a standalone, test.
Raised serum IgG4→Supports IgG4-RD in the right clinical + imaging context
Mild elevation alone→Non-specific — also seen in pancreatic cancer, atopy, other malignancies
Diagnosis rests on a combination of serology, imaging, histology and other-organ involvement — never IgG4 in isolation.
2Type 1 AIP — the classic picture
Typically an older man presenting with painless obstructive jaundice — deliberately cancer-like.
  • Imaging: diffusely enlarged "sausage-shaped" pancreas with a featureless rim (capsule-like halo)
  • Serology: raised serum IgG4
  • Histology: lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate, storiform fibrosis, obliterative phlebitis, abundant IgG4+ plasma cells
Dramatic response to corticosteroids
A steroid trial is used cautiously and only after malignancy has been reasonably excluded.
3AIP vs pancreatic cancer — the great mimic
Both give obstructive jaundice + a pancreatic mass in an older patient, yet management could not differ more: steroids vs Whipple / oncology. Features that favour AIP:
Diffuse "sausage" enlargement→Favours AIP (cancer is usually a focal mass)
Other-organ involvement→Biliary strictures, retroperitoneal fibrosis, salivary/lacrimal enlargement point to IgG4-RD
Raised IgG4 + steroid response→Supportive, but always confirm malignancy is excluded first
4IgG4-RD is multi-system
Look beyond the pancreas — synchronous or metachronous organ involvement is a strong clue to IgG4-RD.
🟡Sclerosing cholangitis
IgG4-related biliary strictures mimicking PSC or cholangiocarcinoma.
🔵Sialadenitis / dacryoadenitis
Salivary and lacrimal gland enlargement (Mikulicz syndrome).
🟢Retroperitoneal fibrosis
Peri-aortic fibrosis that can entrap the ureters.
🟣Tubulointerstitial nephritis
IgG4-related renal disease with impaired function.
🚩
Do not miss malignancy. An obstructive-jaundice pancreatic mass in an older patient is pancreatic cancer until proven otherwise. Never attribute it to AIP on a raised IgG4 alone — a mildly elevated IgG4 also occurs in pancreatic cancer. Exclude malignancy (cross-sectional imaging, EUS ± biopsy, CA 19-9) before giving a steroid trial; missing cancer to treat presumed AIP is a catastrophic error.

IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__Immunoglobulins &:
Serum immunoglobulins (IgG, IgA, IgM; IgE measured separately) quantify the antibody classes, while serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP/SPE) separates serum proteins by charge to detect a monoclonal band (paraprotein / M-spike) in the gamma region. The single most important interpretive skill is distinguishing a broad polyclonal rise (reactive, benign) from a discrete monoclonal band (paraproteinaemia needing a myeloma work-up).
1What the tests measure
Serum Ig levels report the absolute concentration of each class. SPEP resolves serum into albumin, alpha-1, alpha-2, beta and gamma fractions; most antibodies migrate in the gamma region. A discrete spike here is a paraprotein. Immunofixation then types it into a heavy chain plus a single light chain (e.g. IgG kappa), confirming clonality.
SPEP = screenImmunofixation = types the bandSerum free light chainsUrine Bence Jones protein
2Polyclonal vs monoclonal — the key distinction
A polyclonal rise is a broad-based increase across the whole gamma region from many different B-cell clones — this is reactive and benign. A monoclonal band is a single tall discrete spike from one expanded clone — this is paraproteinaemia and needs investigation.
🌊Polyclonal (broad)
Reactive: chronic infection, chronic liver disease, autoimmune/connective tissue disease. No single clone — reassuring.
📈Monoclonal (discrete)
Paraprotein: MGUS, myeloma, Waldenström's (IgM), AL amyloidosis. Needs light chains, urine BJP and CRAB screen.
Discrete gamma spike + low background Igs→Immune paresis — suspect myeloma
Immune paresis: the malignant clone suppresses the uninvolved Ig classes, lowering background IgG/IgA/IgM and driving infection risk.
3Individual class patterns
  • Raised IgE — allergy/atopy and parasitic (helminth) infection.
  • Raised monoclonal IgM — Waldenström's macroglobulinaemia; large IgM pentamers cause hyperviscosity.
  • IgA is the key mucosal antibody — selective IgA deficiency is the commonest primary immunodeficiency (false-negative coeliac serology).
  • Low IgG/IgA/IgM — primary immunodeficiency (e.g. CVID) or secondary (myeloma, drugs, protein loss).
4SPEP in the myeloma work-up
SPEP is the initial screen for a paraprotein, then combined with serum free light chains and urine Bence Jones protein. Myeloma is supported by paraprotein plus end-organ damage (CRAB):
C — hyperCalcaemiaR — Renal impairmentA — AnaemiaB — Bone lesions
A paraprotein with normal background Igs and no CRAB features is likely MGUS, which needs surveillance. See Myeloma ›
🚩
A very high IgM paraprotein (Waldenström's) can cause hyperviscosity syndrome — headache, visual disturbance/retinal changes, mucosal bleeding and confusion. This is an emergency needing urgent haematology referral and plasmapheresis. Also escalate any paraprotein with CRAB features (hypercalcaemia, acute kidney injury).

🎓 Exam pearl. Broad-based gamma rise = polyclonal = reactive (infection, liver disease, autoimmune) — reassure. A discrete monoclonal spike = paraprotein — work up with free light chains, urine Bence Jones and a CRAB screen. Suppressed uninvolved classes = immune paresis, pointing to myeloma over MGUS. A monoclonal IgM means think Waldenström's and hyperviscosity.
The serum free light chain (sFLC) assay measures the small quantities of unbound kappa (κ) and lambda (λ) light chains circulating in serum. The critical readout is the kappa:lambda ratio — a skewed ratio signals a clonal excess of one light chain. Its great strength is detecting light-chain-only and non-secretory myeloma that a normal serum protein electrophoresis would miss.
1What it measures & why the ratio matters
Plasma cells normally produce a small surplus of free light chains alongside intact immunoglobulin. The assay quantifies free κ and free λ separately and calculates the κ:λ ratio (normal roughly 0.26–1.65).
↑ κ:λ ratio = κ clone↓ κ:λ ratio = λ clone
Abnormal (skewed) ratio→Clonal light-chain excess — suspect a monoclonal process
Both κ and λ rising together with a preserved ratio is polyclonal (e.g. inflammation, infection), not clonal.
2The key added value: catching what SPEP misses
In light-chain-only (Bence Jones) and non-secretory myeloma, the malignant clone produces only free light chains and no intact immunoglobulin, so serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP) may show no paraprotein / M-spike. The sFLC assay picks up the clonal excess these cases would otherwise hide.
🔬SPEP + immunofixation
Detects intact monoclonal protein; may be negative in light-chain-only disease.
🔗sFLC assay
Catches light-chain-only / non-secretory clones and gives a quick-responding monitoring marker.
Full myeloma screen = SPEP + immunofixation + sFLC + urinary Bence Jones protein.
3Clinical uses
  • Diagnosis & prognosis of Myeloma › and AL amyloidosis.
  • Monitoring response — sFLC changes faster than SPEP (short serum half-life), so it is a quicker-responding marker of treatment effect.
  • Risk-stratifying MGUS and smouldering myeloma.
4The renal caveat
Free light chains are renally cleared. In renal impairment / CKD, clearance falls and both κ and λ rise, shifting the ratio upward (κ is normally cleared faster, so it accumulates relatively more).
CKD / low eGFR→Use the renal (modified) reference range — do not over-call clonality on a mildly skewed ratio
🚩
Filtered light chains precipitate in the tubules causing cast nephropathy ("myeloma kidney") → acute kidney injury; hypercalcaemia compounds it. New AKI, hypercalcaemia, bone pain or anaemia (the CRAB features) with an abnormal sFLC ratio needs an urgent myeloma work-up — this is a haematological emergency.

🎓 Exam pearl. A patient with AKI, bone pain and a normal SPEP is a classic trap — order the sFLC assay, which reveals a skewed κ:λ ratio in light-chain-only / non-secretory myeloma. Remember the ratio, not the absolute values, is the clonality marker, and that renal failure raises both chains so a renal reference range is used before calling a clone.
The C1 esterase inhibitor (C1-INH) and C4 pathway is the key work-up when you suspect hereditary angioedema (HAE) — recurrent, bradykinin-mediated angioedema occurring without urticaria/wheals and without itch. Getting this right matters because HAE does not respond to the usual anaphylaxis drugs, and attacks involving the airway can be fatal.
1Recognise the picture: bradykinin, not histamine
HAE gives recurrent episodes of non-pitting swelling of the face, lips, tongue, larynx, limbs and gut wall (recurrent unexplained abdominal pain from bowel-wall oedema is classic). The single most useful discriminator from allergic (histaminergic) angioedema:
No urticariaNo itchNo adrenaline response
Wheals + itch, responds to antihistamines/adrenaline→Histamine-mediated (allergic) — not HAE
Swelling without wheals/itch, poor drug response, +FHx→Bradykinin-mediated — screen for HAE
Ask about ACE inhibitors — they potentiate bradykinin and can both cause angioedema and unmask/precipitate HAE attacks (contraindicated).
2Screen with serum C4
Serum C4 is the screening test. It is characteristically LOW both during and between attacks, so a persistently low C4 is a useful, cheap first-line screen. A normal C4 during a symptomatic attack makes HAE very unlikely.
Low C4 (attack and between)→Proceed to C1-INH level + function
3Confirm and classify: C1-INH level, function and C1q
Measure C1-INH antigenic level and C1-INH function; add C1q to separate hereditary from acquired disease.
🧬HAE type 1 (~85%)
Low C1-INH level, low function, low C4, normal C1q.
🧬HAE type 2 (~15%)
Normal/raised C1-INH level but low function, low C4, normal C1q.
⚠️Acquired C1-INH deficiency
Low C1-INH, low C4, but LOW C1q — flags lymphoproliferative/autoimmune disease. Later onset, no FHx.
C1q is the discriminator: normal in hereditary HAE, low in acquired deficiency.
4Why it changes management
Because attacks are bradykinin-mediated, they do not reliably respond to adrenaline, antihistamines or steroids the way allergic angioedema does. Acute treatment is C1-INH concentrate or icatibant (a bradykinin B2-receptor antagonist). Avoid ACE inhibitors lifelong.
  • Acute: C1-INH concentrate / icatibant (± fresh frozen plasma if unavailable).
  • Prophylaxis: attenuated androgens (danazol) or long-term C1-INH.
  • Contraindicated: ACE inhibitors.
🚩
Laryngeal oedema is an airway emergency. Tongue/throat swelling with voice change, stridor or dysphagia can obstruct the airway within minutes and is not reliably reversed by adrenaline, antihistamines or steroids in HAE. Secure the airway early and give C1-INH concentrate or icatibant without delay.

Serum mast cell tryptase is a protease released when mast cells degranulate, so a transient rise in the blood supports (retrospectively confirms) anaphylaxis or mast-cell activation. Crucially, anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis — never delay IM adrenaline to wait for a tryptase level. See Anaphylaxis ›
1What the test tells you
Tryptase peaks in the blood after mast-cell degranulation and then falls back to baseline. It is the key retrospective confirmatory test for a suspected anaphylactic or mast-cell activation event — it does not change acute management.
Confirms mast-cell activationGuides allergy referralScreens for mastocytosis
Dynamic rise then fall→Supports anaphylaxis
2Timed serial samples
A single value means little — the diagnosis rests on a dynamic rise-and-fall against the patient's own baseline. Take three timed samples:
⏱️Sample 1 — ASAP
As soon as feasible after resuscitation has started — do NOT delay treatment to take it.
📈Sample 2 — 1–2 h
1–2 hours after symptom onset — captures the expected peak.
🟰Sample 3 — baseline
≥24 h later or in convalescence — confirms return to baseline.
Serum sample; label each tube with the exact time taken.
3Interpreting the result
  • A normal tryptase does not exclude anaphylaxis — it may stay normal, especially in food-triggered or normotensive reactions.
  • Drug and venom triggers, and hypotensive reactions, more reliably raise it.
  • A persistently elevated baseline (Sample 3 still high) suggests an underlying mast cell disorder — systemic mastocytosis or hereditary alpha-tryptasaemia — and warrants specialist referral.
Baseline stays high→Refer: ? mastocytosis
🚩
Anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis — give IM adrenaline immediately and never delay it to obtain tryptase. A raised baseline tryptase that fails to settle must be referred to allergy/immunology for mastocytosis — a commonly missed follow-up.

Skin prick testing (SPT) and specific IgE (the old RAST) are first-line investigations for Type I (IgE-mediated) hypersensitivity — the immediate reactions behind allergic rhinitis, food allergy, drug allergy and anaphylaxis. Both detect sensitisation (the presence of allergen-specific IgE), which is not the same as clinical allergy; a result is only meaningful when read against the patient's history.
1Skin prick test (SPT)
Standardised allergen extracts are placed on the volar forearm and a lancet pricks the skin through each drop. Read at 15 minutes: a wheal ≥3 mm larger than the negative control counts as positive. Two controls are mandatory — histamine (positive) confirms the skin can react, saline (negative) excludes dermatographism.
CheapQuick (15 min)SensitiveResult at the bedside
Antihistamines not stopped→false negatives — stop 3–5 days before
Small risk of a systemic reaction — only perform where resuscitation facilities are available.
2Specific IgE (formerly RAST)
A blood test that measures the concentration of allergen-specific IgE in serum. It is not affected by antihistamines and carries no risk of a systemic reaction, but it is more expensive and results take days. Choose it when SPT is impractical or unsafe.
💊Antihistamines can't stop
Chronic urticaria or unavoidable antihistamine use — bloods are unaffected.
🩹Skin unavailable
Extensive eczema or dermatographism makes SPT uninterpretable.
⚠️High anaphylaxis risk
Previous severe reaction — avoid exposing the patient to allergen in the skin.
🧒Uncooperative patient
Young children or those unable to keep still for skin testing.
3Interpretation — sensitisation ≠ allergy
This is the point examiners test. A positive SPT or specific IgE proves only that the patient has made IgE to that allergen — asymptomatic sensitisation is common. The result is only clinically relevant if it matches the history of a reproducible, temporally-linked reaction.
  • Do not diagnose allergy on a positive test alone, and do not eliminate foods from the diet on the basis of a test without a matching history — needless elimination risks malnutrition and can even promote new allergy.
  • Larger wheals / higher specific IgE raise the probability of true allergy but never confirm it.
  • Total IgE gives context (e.g. atopy, parasitic infection) but does not identify the culprit.
  • Component-resolved diagnostics measure IgE to individual allergen proteins (e.g. Ara h 2 in peanut) to refine risk and cross-reactivity.
Genuine diagnostic uncertainty→supervised oral food/drug challenge — the gold standard
🚩
Both tests carry a small but real risk of triggering a systemic reaction (especially SPT). Perform only where adrenaline and resuscitation are immediately available, and treat any evolving airway, breathing or circulatory compromise as Anaphylaxis ›.

In suspected allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA), serology is the diagnostic cornerstone. ABPA is a hypersensitivity reaction to Aspergillus fumigatus colonising the airways, classically in asthma and cystic fibrosis. Suspect it in poorly-controlled or steroid-dependent asthma with recurrent exacerbations, wheeze, cough productive of brownish mucus plugs, and fleeting CXR infiltrates. The key tests are a markedly raised total IgE, Aspergillus-specific IgE (with skin prick positivity) and Aspergillus IgG/precipitins, backed by peripheral eosinophilia.
1The core serology panel
Three antibody/eosinophil markers work together to confirm ABPA:
📈Total IgE
Markedly raised, usually >1000 IU/mL. Also used to monitor disease activity and treatment response.
🍄Aspergillus IgE + skin test
Raised specific IgE / positive skin prick = immediate type I hypersensitivity. The entry criterion for ABPA.
🧫Aspergillus IgG / precipitins
Positive = type III response. Supports the diagnosis but is not specific for ABPA (see step 2).
🩸Blood eosinophilia
Peripheral eosinophil count typically raised (often >0.5 × 10⁹/L), reflecting the allergic response.
2IgE vs IgG — don't confuse them
The distinction is a classic exam trap:
Aspergillus IgE / positive skin test→Hallmark of ABPA (allergic, type I)
Aspergillus IgG / precipitins alone→Also seen in chronic pulmonary aspergillosis & aspergilloma (mycetoma)
IgE = allergicIgG = colonisation/invasion
IgG positivity supports ABPA only in the right context — raised total IgE, specific IgE and eosinophilia. IgG alone is not diagnostic of ABPA.
3Imaging & management context
  • Imaging: central/proximal bronchiectasis and mucoid impaction; fleeting infiltrates on CXR.
  • Treatment: oral corticosteroids are the mainstay, ± antifungal (itraconazole) to reduce fungal burden.
  • Monitoring: falling total IgE tracks response; a rising level suggests relapse.
  • Untreated: progresses to fixed bronchiectasis and pulmonary fibrosis.
Related: Asthma › Bronchiectasis ›
🚩
Consider ABPA in any poorly-controlled or steroid-dependent asthmatic. It is under-recognised, and if missed causes progressive bronchiectasis and pulmonary fibrosis. A total IgE >1000 IU/mL with positive Aspergillus IgE in an asthmatic should prompt urgent specialist referral.

🎓 Exam pearl. The ABPA triad to quote: markedly raised total IgE (>1000), positive Aspergillus-specific IgE / skin prick test, and eosinophilia, on a background of asthma or CF. Remember IgE = allergic ABPA (entry criterion) while IgG/precipitins also appear in aspergilloma and chronic pulmonary aspergillosis, so IgG alone is not specific. Total IgE is the key monitoring marker.
Lymphocyte subset analysis (immunophenotyping by flow cytometry) enumerates the main lymphocyte populations in blood: CD4+ T-helper, CD8+ cytotoxic T, CD19/CD20+ B cells and CD16/CD56+ NK cells. It is the key investigation for suspected immunodeficiency (primary and secondary) and for staging and monitoring HIV. The pattern of which subset is depleted points to the diagnosis.
1The four subsets and what they mean
Each population carries characteristic surface CD (cluster of differentiation) markers used to gate cells on the cytometer.
🧫CD4+ T-helper
Coordinates adaptive immunity; the HIV target cell and key marker of immune status.
🧫CD8+ cytotoxic T
Kills virus-infected/tumour cells; rises in HIV, inverting the CD4:CD8 ratio.
🧫CD19/CD20+ B cells
Antibody production. Absent/low → agammaglobulinaemia (e.g. X-linked Bruton's).
🧫CD16/CD56+ NK cells
Innate cytotoxicity; presence/absence helps subtype SCID.
2HIV: CD4 count and CD4:CD8 ratio
The CD4 count is the central marker of immune status in HIV and falls as disease progresses.
HIV progresses→CD4 falls, CD8 rises → ratio inverts (normal ~2:1 → <1)
On ART→CD4 monitors immune recovery; viral load monitors virological response
CD4 >500 reassuringCD4 200–500 moderate riskCD4 <200 AIDS-level risk
See HIV › for staging and antiretroviral therapy.
3Primary immunodeficiency: read the pattern
Which subset is missing localises the defect.
  • Absent/low B cells → agammaglobulinaemia (e.g. X-linked / Bruton's) — recurrent bacterial infections, low immunoglobulins.
  • Low T cells → DiGeorge syndrome (thymic aplasia; 22q11 deletion, hypocalcaemia, cardiac defects).
  • Low T ± B ± NK → SCID — subtype (e.g. T−B+NK−, T−B−NK+) depends on the genetic cause; a paediatric emergency.
4Pitfalls in interpretation
Counts are age-dependent — children have physiologically higher lymphocyte and CD4 counts, so always use age-adjusted reference ranges. Values also fluctuate with acute illness, corticosteroids and diurnal variation, so interpret a single result in clinical context and repeat when stable if borderline.
🚩
CD4 <200 cells/µL is the AIDS-defining threshold and marks high risk of opportunistic infection. Start PCP (Pneumocystis jirovecii) prophylaxis with co-trimoxazole and consider further prophylaxis as CD4 falls. In an infant, absent T cells (± B/NK) suggests SCID — a paediatric emergency: refer urgently, avoid live vaccines and give only irradiated/CMV-negative blood products.

🎓 Exam pearl. CD4 count = immune status; viral load = virological response. CD4 <200 → AIDS-defining, start co-trimoxazole PCP prophylaxis. HIV inverts the CD4:CD8 ratio (normal ~2:1 → <1). In immunodeficiency, the missing subset names the disease: no B cells = Bruton's, low T = DiGeorge, low T±B±NK = SCID (paediatric emergency).
The NBT (nitroblue tetrazolium) and DHR (dihydrorhodamine) tests assess the neutrophil oxidative (respiratory) burst. They are the definitive investigations for chronic granulomatous disease (CGD), a primary immunodeficiency in which a defective NADPH oxidase leaves phagocytes unable to generate reactive oxygen species to kill ingested microbes.
1The defect being tested
In CGD, NADPH oxidase in neutrophils and macrophages is defective, so cells cannot produce the superoxide / reactive oxygen species of the respiratory burst. Phagocytes still ingest microbes but cannot kill them, driving recurrent deep-seated infections and granuloma formation. Inheritance is most commonly X-linked (gp91-phox), so classically affects boys.
NADPH oxidase defectNo respiratory burstX-linked (commonest)
2NBT and DHR: how to read them
Both tests ask a single question: can the neutrophil mount an oxidative burst?
  • NBT test — normal neutrophils reduce yellow NBT dye to blue formazan. In CGD they cannot, so the dye stays yellow/colourless (abnormal result).
  • DHR flow cytometry — the modern, more sensitive and quantitative test. Normal neutrophils oxidise DHR to fluorescent rhodamine; CGD neutrophils show absent/reduced fluorescence.
Normal neutrophil→NBT turns blue / DHR fluoresces
CGD neutrophil→NBT stays yellow / DHR flat
DHR is now preferred over NBT: quantitative, better at detecting carriers and mild/residual-activity variants.
3Which organisms — and management
CGD patients are vulnerable to catalase-positive organisms, which destroy their own hydrogen peroxide so the phagocyte cannot borrow it to kill them.
🦠Staph aureus
Classic bacterial culprit — skin, lymph node and liver abscesses.
🍄Aspergillus
Invasive fungal infection — a leading cause of death in CGD.
🧫Others
Serratia, Burkholderia (cepacia), Nocardia — also catalase-positive.
Co-trimoxazole (antibacterial prophylaxis)Itraconazole (antifungal prophylaxis)Interferon-γHSCT = definitive
🚩
Suspect invasive aspergillosis in any CGD patient with fever, pleuritic chest pain or a new lung lesion — invasive fungal infection is a leading cause of death in CGD. Ensure antifungal prophylaxis (itraconazole) is in place and escalate urgently; do not wait for classic bacterial signs.

🎓 Exam pearl. CGD = NADPH oxidase defect → no respiratory burst. NBT stays yellow (fails to turn blue); DHR shows absent fluorescence and is the modern test of choice. Think catalase-positive organisms — Staph aureus and Aspergillus — with recurrent abscesses and granulomas. See the Immunodeficiency › overview for context.
Vaccine (test-immunisation) antibody responses assess the function of the humoral immune system, not merely the level of immunoglobulins. Baseline specific antibody titres are measured against past vaccines; if low, a test vaccine is given and titres re-checked after ~4 weeks to see whether the patient can mount and sustain a protective response. The core principle: a normal total IgG does not guarantee functioning antibody — a patient can have near-normal immunoglobulins yet fail to make protective specific antibody.
1Why test function, not just level
Total immunoglobulin assays measure quantity; test vaccination measures quality — can the B-cell/antibody system actually respond to antigen? A poor or absent titre rise after a booster indicates a functional antibody deficiency (e.g. CVID, specific antibody deficiency) even when total IgG, IgA and IgM look near-normal. This is the single most examined concept: function > level.
Baseline titres too high to interpret? A booster gives a <2-fold rise in already-immune patients, so falling titres are re-tested against the pre-vaccine baseline.
2Two antigen types — protein vs polysaccharide
Two mechanistically different antigens probe different arms of the antibody response:
💉Protein antigen
Tetanus / diphtheria toxoid — a T-cell-DEPENDENT response. Tests classic CD4-helped B-cell antibody production and memory.
🧫Polysaccharide antigen
Unconjugated pneumococcal polysaccharide (Pneumovax / PPV23) — a T-cell-INDEPENDENT response. Selective failure here (with normal protein responses) points to specific polysaccharide antibody deficiency.
Normal tetanus rise + absent pneumococcal rise→Specific polysaccharide antibody deficiency
3When it is used & what it guides
Part of the work-up of recurrent bacterial infections, especially sinopulmonary infection with encapsulated organisms (pneumococcus, Haemophilus influenzae) — the very organisms handled by anti-polysaccharide antibody.
Recurrent pneumonia/sinusitisEncapsulated bacteriaGuides Ig replacement
  • A demonstrated failure to respond supports the decision to start immunoglobulin replacement.
  • Use conjugate vs unconjugated pneumococcal vaccines appropriately — conjugate (Prevenar) recruits T-cell help and can restore responses.
  • Do not interpret responses taken during immunosuppression — steroids, rituximab and chemotherapy blunt titres and produce false results.
Immunodeficiency ›
🚩
Live vaccines are contraindicated in significant immunodeficiency (e.g. suspected CVID, SCID, agammaglobulinaemia) — they can cause disseminated vaccine-strain infection. Use inactivated/toxoid and polysaccharide/conjugate vaccines only for test immunisation, and never give a live vaccine to a patient under active investigation for antibody deficiency until immune competence is confirmed.

🎓 Exam pearl. Function beats level — a patient with normal total IgG who fails to raise specific antibody after a test vaccine has a functional antibody deficiency. Protein (tetanus/diphtheria toxoid) = T-cell-dependent; polysaccharide (Pneumovax/PPV23) = T-cell-independent. Isolated failure of polysaccharide responses = specific polysaccharide antibody deficiency. Never interpret results during immunosuppression, and never give live vaccines to a patient with significant immunodeficiency.
IMMUNOLOGY / SEROLOGY__Infection & Immun:
Viral serology asks one question in many disguises: is this infection acute, chronic, past, or immune? The trick is matching antigens (the virus is here now) against antibody classes — IgM for recent/acute and IgG for past exposure or immunity. The hepatitis B panel is the classic finals interpretation, but the same IgM/IgG logic decodes hepatitis A/E, HIV, EBV and CMV. See Viral hepatitis A–E › and HIV ›.
1Hepatitis B panel — the exam classic
Learn each marker, then the combinations:
HBsAg = current infection (acute or chronic)anti-HBs = immunity (vaccine OR cleared)anti-HBc IgM = acute/recentanti-HBc IgG (total core) = natural infection, past or presentHBeAg / HBV DNA = high infectivity/replication
Key rule: vaccine gives anti-HBs ONLY. If anti-HBc is positive, the patient met the real virus, not the jab.
💉Vaccinated
anti-HBs +; HBsAg −, anti-HBc − (core-negative = never natural infection).
✅Past cleared infection
anti-HBs + AND anti-HBc +; HBsAg − (immune by natural resolution).
⚠️Chronic infection
HBsAg + for >6 months, anti-HBc +, anti-HBs −. Check HBeAg/DNA for infectivity.
🦠Acute infection
HBsAg + with anti-HBc IgM +; HBeAg often + (highly infectious).
2Hepatitis C, D and the A/E pair
  • Hepatitis C: anti-HCV antibody = exposure (past or present). Confirm active infection with HCV RNA (PCR).
  • Hepatitis D (delta): defective virus — only co-infects/superinfects when HBsAg +. Test anti-HDV in any HBsAg-positive patient.
  • Hepatitis A & E: mainly acute, self-limiting, faeco-oral. IgM = acute, IgG = past/immune. Hep E is dangerous in pregnancy and the immunocompromised.
anti-HCV + , HCV RNA −→Cleared or successfully treated infection (no active virus)
anti-HCV + , HCV RNA +→Active chronic hepatitis C — refer for direct-acting antivirals
3HIV screening and the window period
The UK screening test is the 4th-generation combined antigen/antibody assay — it detects p24 antigen plus anti-HIV antibody. Including p24 shortens the window period (the seroconversion delay between infection and detectable antibody), so it turns positive earlier than antibody-only tests.
Reactive screen → must be confirmedWindow period = seroconversion delayRepeat at 45 days if early exposure
A reactive result is a screen, not a diagnosis — always confirm before telling a patient they are HIV positive.
4EBV and CMV — the mononucleosis pair
  • EBV (infectious mononucleosis): screen with the heterophile antibody test (Monospot / Paul-Bunnell). EBV-specific serology: VCA IgM = acute; VCA IgG and EBNA IgG = past infection/immunity (EBNA appears late, so its presence argues against a very recent infection).
  • CMV: IgM = acute, IgG = past. A heterophile-negative glandular-fever picture is often CMV. Critical in pregnancy (congenital CMV), transplant and the immunocompromised.
Monospot can be falsely negative in the first week and in young children — repeat or use EBV-specific serology.
🚩
After a needlestick / occupational exposure, act urgently: assess source and recipient, give hepatitis B post-exposure prophylaxis (booster ± HBIG) based on vaccination/anti-HBs status, and start HIV PEP within hours (ideally <1h, up to 72h). Separately, suspect fulminant (acute liver failure) hepatitis — worse with Hep B+D or Hep E in pregnancy — if a jaundiced patient develops encephalopathy or coagulopathy (rising INR); discuss immediately with a liver unit.

🎓 Exam pearl. For hepatitis B, read anti-HBc first: negative core = the patient only ever met the vaccine (anti-HBs +, all else −); positive core = they met the real virus. Then HBsAg splits current (positive) from resolved (negative), and anti-HBs tells you if they are now immune. For hepatitis C, antibody = exposure, RNA = active infection. Across all viruses: IgM acute, IgG past/immune.
The Mantoux test (tuberculin skin test, TST) and IGRA (interferon-gamma release assay) both detect a cell-mediated (type IV / T-cell) immune response to Mycobacterium tuberculosis. They identify TB infection — usually latent TB — but cannot distinguish latent from active disease, and neither confirms nor excludes active TB on its own. See Tuberculosis ›.
1Mantoux (tuberculin skin test)
An intradermal injection of tuberculin PPD into the forearm. Read the induration (the raised firm area) — not erythema — at 48-72 hours, measured transversely in millimetres. Interpreted against risk-stratified thresholds:
  • ≥5 mm — HIV, immunosuppressed, recent close contacts.
  • ≥10 mm — most other at-risk groups (new entrants, healthcare workers).
  • ≥15 mm — low-risk individuals.
False positive: prior BCG vaccinationFalse positive: non-tuberculous mycobacteria
False negative: immunosuppression / HIVFalse negative: very young ageFalse negative: miliary / overwhelming TB (anergy)
2IGRA (QuantiFERON-TB Gold, T-SPOT.TB)
A blood test measuring interferon-gamma release by the patient's T-cells after stimulation with TB-specific antigens ESAT-6 and CFP-10. Crucially these antigens are NOT present in BCG, so IGRA is not confounded by prior BCG vaccination — its key advantage over Mantoux — and is largely unaffected by non-tuberculous mycobacteria.
Prior BCG + positive Mantoux→confirm with IGRA (BCG does not cause a positive IGRA)
Only requires a single visit (no return for reading), but is more expensive and needs a lab.
3Clinical use — screening for latent TB
Used to screen for latent TB infection in defined groups. A positive test in someone who is well and asymptomatic = latent TB, prompting consideration of chemoprophylaxis (e.g. isoniazid + rifampicin).
👥Contacts
Close contacts of active pulmonary TB cases.
💊Pre-immunosuppression
Before biologics (anti-TNF), transplant or chemotherapy.
🌍New entrants / HCW
Migrants from high-incidence areas; healthcare worker screening.
Active TB requires clinical + radiological assessment plus microbiology — sputum smear, culture and NAAT — never IGRA/Mantoux alone.
🚩
Never use a negative IGRA or Mantoux to exclude active TB, and never rely on a positive one to diagnose it. In a symptomatic patient a positive test still needs sputum microscopy, culture and NAAT — and a negative test does NOT rule out active TB, especially in immunosuppression, HIV or miliary/overwhelming disease where anergy causes false negatives. Treat the clinical picture, not the immunology result.

🎓 Exam pearl. Both tests detect infection, not disease — they cannot tell latent from active TB. Mantoux measures induration at 48-72h (not erythema) and is falsely positive after BCG; IGRA uses ESAT-6 / CFP-10 antigens absent from BCG, so it is not confounded by vaccination. A positive test in a well person = latent TB (consider chemoprophylaxis); a positive test in a symptomatic person still needs sputum culture + NAAT.
The immunobullous antibodies are the serological fingerprint that separates the two great autoimmune blistering diseases: pemphigus (antibodies to desmoglein, glue between keratinocytes) and pemphigoid (antibodies to BP180/BP230, anchors at the base of the epidermis). Getting the target antigen right tells you the level of the split, the blister character, and how sick the patient is.
1The two antibody targets
Autoantibodies attack adhesion proteins. Where the protein sits determines where the skin splits.
🫧Desmoglein 3 (± Dsg1)
Pemphigus vulgaris. Dsg3 holds keratinocytes together at desmosomes. Loss of adhesion (acantholysis) causes an intra-epidermal split. Dsg3 = mucosa; Dsg1 = skin — so mucosal disease first, then skin as anti-Dsg1 appears.
🧱BP180 & BP230
Bullous pemphigoid. Hemidesmosome proteins (BP180 = BPAG2; BP230 = BPAG1) anchor basal keratinocytes to the basement membrane. Attack here gives a sub-epidermal split. Anti-BP180 correlates best with disease activity.
2How the lab confirms it
Two complementary tests, always on the right sample:
  • Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) on perilesional skin — the gold standard. Shows where the antibody is deposited.
  • Serum antibodies by ELISA (anti-Dsg1, anti-Dsg3, anti-BP180, anti-BP230) — confirm the target and monitor disease activity/relapse.
  • H&E histology of a fresh blister — shows the level of the split (intra- vs sub-epidermal).
Pemphigus DIF: intercellular IgG — "chicken-wire"/fishnetPemphigoid DIF: linear IgG + C3 along basement membrane
Tip: biopsy perilesional (not the blister centre) for DIF — the roof and floor of an old blister lose antigen.
3Side-by-side discriminator
The classic finals comparison — antigen, split, blister, mucosa, Nikolsky, DIF:
Anti-Dsg3, intra-epidermal, flaccid painful blisters, mucosa++, Nikolsky POSITIVE→Pemphigus vulgaris (fishnet IgG)
Anti-BP180/230, sub-epidermal, TENSE itchy blisters, elderly, mucosa spared, Nikolsky NEGATIVE→Bullous pemphigoid (linear IgG/C3)
Memory hook: pemphigUS = flaccid + Nikolsky positive + mucosa; pemphigOID = tense + "deeper" sub-epidermal + elderly. See Immunobullous disorders ›
🚩
Pemphigus vulgaris can be life-threatening. Extensive flaccid blisters and painful erosions behave like a burn — fluid and protein loss, electrolyte disturbance, and secondary bacterial infection/sepsis. Widespread mucosal erosions cause severe pain and poor oral intake. Refer urgently to dermatology; these patients may need admission and systemic immunosuppression.

🎓 Exam pearl. Match the antibody to the layer: Desmoglein → desmosome → intra-epidermal → flaccid, Nikolsky positive, mucosa (pemphigus); BP180/BP230 → hemidesmosome → sub-epidermal → tense, Nikolsky negative, elderly (pemphigoid). DIF on perilesional skin is the gold standard; ELISA titres (esp. anti-Dsg3 / anti-BP180) confirm the target and track disease activity.
